uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; detectability/unawareness concern is that users may not expect these secondary uses.

title: Secondary guardian can link live location data to a specific child and household
description: By granting access and sharing the child's live location with the secondary guardian, the backend enables direct association of precise location updates with an identified child and their family context. This creates a linkability risk if the recipient can correlate repeated updates over time or combine them with other account information.
assumptions: Assumes the shared live location is tied to an identifiable child account rather than being fully anonymized or heavily obfuscated.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node ids.

title: Live location disclosure to an over-privileged or unintended secondary guardian
description: The backend discloses highly sensitive real-time location data to the secondary guardian. If access is granted without strong authorization checks, correct relationship validation, or appropriate scoping, the child’s whereabouts may be exposed to someone who should not receive them or to a recipient with broader access than necessary.
assumptions: Assumes there is some possibility of misconfiguration, stale permissions, account compromise, or insufficient role validation when granting secondary-guardian access.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Insufficient evidence of who granted and accessed location-sharing rights
description: If the backend does not maintain trustworthy records of consent, delegation, access grants, and subsequent location accesses, parties may later deny that access was granted or that live location was viewed. This undermines accountability for privacy-relevant disclosures involving the child’s location.
assumptions: Assumes audit logging, consent records, or access receipts may be absent, incomplete, or not tamper-evident.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies if accountability mechanisms are weak; exact node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian can infer sensitive habits and routines from live location stream
description: Continuous or repeated sharing of the child's live location allows the recipient to derive private information beyond raw coordinates, such as home and school addresses, daily routines, religious attendance, medical visits, social relationships, and periods when the child is alone or vulnerable.
assumptions: Assumes location is shared with sufficient precision and frequency to reveal patterns over time.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate; inference risk is strongly supported by the nature of live location data.

title: Child may be unaware that live location is being shared with a secondary guardian
description: If the backend grants secondary-guardian access without clear, timely notice to the child or primary guardian, the data subject may not know that real-time location is being disclosed, to whom, and under what conditions. This creates a detectability risk around the existence and scope of the sharing.
assumptions: Assumes the system may not provide transparent in-app indicators, notifications, or dashboards showing active location-sharing recipients.
uncertainty_note: Detectability in LINDDUN can be nuanced here; exact node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian may be unable to understand limits and consequences of location access
description: If the backend or associated UI does not clearly communicate what 'access' entails, how live location is updated, retention expectations, onward sharing restrictions, and revocation behavior, the recipient and affected guardians may misunderstand the privacy impact of enabling this flow.
assumptions: Assumes notices or explanations about live-location sharing may be incomplete, ambiguous, or hard to access.
uncertainty_note: Usability threat depends partly on surrounding UI and notices, not solely the backend flow; included because the backend grants the access underlying the sharing.

title: Location sharing with secondary guardian may occur without valid consent or proper legal basis
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to a child's live location may violate consent, parental authorization, custody constraints, purpose limitation, or data-minimization requirements if the backend enables sharing without verifying that the disclosure is lawful and aligned with applicable policy and jurisdictional obligations.
assumptions: Assumes child location data is regulated personal data and that secondary-guardian access may require explicit authorization, documented consent, or other legal checks.
uncertainty_note: Exact compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and product context; node id is approximate.

title: Partner can link aggregated analytics to other datasets
description: Even if the backend shares only aggregated usage and engagement analytics, the advertising/analytics partner may combine segment-level metrics, campaign data, device/network metadata, timestamps, app version, geography, or publisher identifiers with its own large cross-service datasets to link the shared data back to particular users or small cohorts. This creates a linkability risk arising from disclosure on this flow.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include dimensions or breakdowns fine-grained enough to enable joins or singling out when combined with partner-held data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types for Process->ExternalEntity but not detailed threat-tree node ids.

title: Aggregated analytics may still reveal user interests or behavior patterns
description: Shared engagement analytics can expose sensitive inferences about users or user groups, such as interests, habits, demographics, or app usage patterns. If aggregation thresholds are low or dimensions are detailed, the partner may infer information about identifiable or nearly identifiable individuals.
assumptions: Assumes analytics include behavioral dimensions, cohort breakdowns, or sparse segments rather than only very coarse global totals.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends strongly on aggregation granularity and whether small-cell suppression or differential privacy-like controls are absent.

title: Partner may detect presence of a user's activity in shared analytics
description: If the backend shares near-real-time or narrowly segmented analytics, the partner may be able to determine whether a particular user's activity contributed to a metric by observing changes across time windows, campaigns, regions, or other slices. This is a detectability threat even when direct identifiers are omitted.
assumptions: Assumes frequent reporting, small cohorts, or differencing across reports is possible.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is moderate but depends on reporting cadence and minimum cohort sizes.

title: Shared analytics may enable disclosure through small groups or differencing
description: Aggregation alone does not guarantee anonymity. If the backend shares metrics for small cohorts, rare events, or multiple overlapping slices, the partner may reconstruct information about individuals or disclose personal data through differencing attacks and repeated observations.
assumptions: Assumes insufficient k-anonymity thresholds, overlapping segment exports, or lack of noise injection/suppression.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; the substantive threat is disclosure of information despite aggregation.

title: Users may be unaware that analytics are shared with an advertising partner
description: Users of the free tier may not realize that backend analytics are disclosed to an external advertising/analytics partner to support monetization. If this sharing is not clearly communicated, users cannot understand who receives data and for what purpose, creating an unawareness threat.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices, in-app disclosures, or just-in-time explanations are incomplete, unclear, or not salient.
uncertainty_note: This threat is strong given the monetization purpose, but exact applicability depends on the quality of user-facing disclosures.

title: Analytics sharing for advertising may exceed consent or lawful-purpose expectations
description: Sending usage and engagement analytics to an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier may be incompatible with the user's original expectations, consent choices, or the declared purpose of collection. If users did not validly consent or cannot object where required, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the app is subject to privacy laws or platform rules requiring transparency, purpose limitation, consent, opt-out, or contractual controls for third-party analytics/advertising sharing.
uncertainty_note: Legal/compliance applicability depends on jurisdiction, consent design, contract terms, and whether the partner acts as processor/service provider or independent third party.

title: Check-in/SOS message and location can be linked to the child across events
description: The manual check-in/SOS payload contains the child's current location and is sent from the child's account/device to the backend. Repeated submissions can be linked to the same child, enabling reconstruction of movement patterns and behavioral profiles over time.
assumptions: The backend receives a stable account, device, session, or other identifier together with the message, or can otherwise associate repeated messages with the same child.

title: SOS/check-in content identifies the child and reveals precise whereabouts
description: The flow carries highly identifying and sensitive information: the child is the sender of a manual check-in/SOS event and the message includes current location. This directly reveals the child's identity or account association together with real-time whereabouts.

title: Attributed SOS/check-in records may prevent the child from plausibly denying having sent them
description: The backend may store message records, timestamps, account identifiers, device metadata, and location as evidence that a particular child initiated a check-in or SOS. Such attributable records can later be used to prove the child sent the message, reducing plausible deniability.
assumptions: The backend logs or persists the event with identifiers and metadata sufficient to attribute it to the child.

title: The flow discloses sensitive personal data beyond what may be strictly necessary
description: A manual check-in/SOS message with current location exposes sensitive contextual information about the child, including real-time whereabouts and potentially distress/emergency status. If precise location, rich metadata, or unnecessary fields are transmitted, the flow increases disclosure risk.
assumptions: The payload includes precise coordinates and/or metadata such as timestamp, device identifiers, message text, or status flags.

assumptions: The backend stores or can analyze multiple events over time rather than treating each message ephemerally.
